newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Deng death could hit China economy - newspaper.
newsitem.headline: Deng death could hit China economy - newspaper.

text.p: The death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping could slow down China's economy as President Jiang Zemin compromises on key issues to keep his job, Singapore's Business Times newspaper said on Friday.

"The situation is near critical on many fronts -- loss-making state enterprises, under-investment in the agricultural sector, overbuilding in the cities, lack of a uniform body of business legislation, corruption, to name but a few," wrote columnist Lee Han Shih
"If the economy is to continue to grow, Mr Jiang and his team need to tackle these problems immediately. This might not happen," he said.
"Deprived of Mr Deng's powerful backing, he may have to make large compromises with the ruling factions (the military, the conservatives, the provincial bosses, etc) to keep his job," Lee said.

After Deng's death late on Wednesday, Jiang, who is also Communist Party Chief and head of the army, was widely expected to hold the reins of power, at least until the Chinese communist party's 15th Congress due in October.
But analysts said Chinese leaders have already been jockeying for position behind the scenes and power struggles could be on the way.

"If Mr Jiang takes the necessary hard approach and exposes (state enterprises) to market forces, literally millions could lose their jobs. The repercussions of such a move would be felt all the way to Beijing and threaten Mr Jiang's own position -- if he is allowed to make it in the first place," he added.
"Multiply the situation many times and it is clear that while Mr Jiang is in name the supreme leader, in fact he has little room for manoeuvring."
Lee said Jiang would have to wait at least until the Communist Party Congress in October to make key decisions, and that this would create uncertainty.

"The Chinese economy -- and by extension stock markets in Hong Kong, Shanghai, Shenzhen and even Taiwan -- will be hit by some political uncertainty for a period that could last for anything from eight months to a few years," he said.
"Business thrives on predictability. A country whose policies can change from day to day is unlikely to attract much foreign investment -- money China badly needs for its economic reform," Lee said.

"If Mr Jiang does not get a grip on the economy soon, not only will China find it hard to attract further foreign funds, it might also stand in danger of losing some of the vast amounts that are already invested in the country."
